global.headline: Budget office puts the Iran war at US$38bn and two-thirds of interceptors
summary: The Congressional Budget Office put US combat operations against Iran at about US$38 billion through 1 August, most of it the US$21.7 billion to replace munitions. The war has consumed half to two-thirds of American stocks of certain missile-defence interceptors since June 2025 — inventories needing at least five years to rebuild even at raised production. The Pentagon's inspector general separately confirmed strategic shortfalls and industrial-base bottlenecks in resupply, against Trump's claim that supplies are "virtually limitless".

In the strait, Oman towed the Panama-flagged El Gaia to port, 23 crew rescued and two missing; the IRGC said mines, CENTCOM said a missile then a drone. Brent traded near US$107.50, a four-month high, the East-West pipeline still shut.
global.geopolitical: Depletion is now a constraint on policy rather than an accounting note. An administration weighing deeper strikes on hardened Iranian sites is being told by its own budget office that the magazines behind that threat take five years to refill.
global.socioeconomic: The CBO expects the war to push up US inflation. With the East-West pipeline offline there is no large export route out of the Gulf that avoids Hormuz — which is why Brent sits above US$107 instead of easing.

global.headline: NATO downs an armed drone over Lithuania as Dutch rail is sabotaged
summary: NATO fighters shot down a drone that crossed into Lithuanian airspace, most likely from Belarus — the first such interception over the country. Bomb-disposal teams found an explosive device on it and neutralised it. Off Denmark, a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish Fennec helicopter photographing it in international waters, narrowly missing the aircraft; the Kremlin did not comment.

In the Netherlands, ProRail reported signalling faults at more than 30 locations from 05:30 on Budget Day, caused by pipes fastened to the tracks and jumper cables faking occupied sections. Much of the national network stopped through the morning commute and a train struck one of the affected sections near Steenwijk without injuries. Nobody has claimed the sabotage.
global.geopolitical: Ursula von der Leyen called the episodes a pattern rather than isolated incidents, which is the hard part: each act sits deliberately below the Article 5 threshold, and the alliance has no agreed answer to a campaign designed never to cross it.
global.socioeconomic: Rail, power and cable operators across Europe now carry a security cost they never priced. A morning of signalling faults halted a national network using hardware worth almost nothing — the asymmetry is the point, and insurers will follow.

global.headline: US confirms it has weapons in orbit, a first for any official
summary: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference at National Harbor, Maryland that "the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action" — the first public acknowledgement by a Pentagon official of a capability long assumed and never admitted. He gave no detail on the type of weapon or when it was deployed; the possibilities run from directed-energy systems and cyber payloads to kinetic interceptors.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit but says nothing about conventional ones. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said space must stay free of any weapons and called for moves toward complete demilitarisation.
global.geopolitical: Washington has traded ambiguity for deterrence. Saying it aloud lets Moscow and Beijing acknowledge their own systems without cost, and hands them a ready argument at the UN that the treaty's silence on conventional weapons now needs filling.
global.socioeconomic: Low Earth orbit carries navigation, weather, communications and the timing signals finance runs on. Debris from one kinetic engagement persists for years and can cascade, so the commercial exposure is far wider than the militaries involved.

global.headline: Supreme Court blocks Trump's mail-ballot rule for the November midterms
summary: The Supreme Court refused to let the administration enforce a Postal Service mail-ballot rule in November, dividing 7-2 with Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissenting. The rule, issued in late August under an executive order, would have required states to redesign ballot envelopes with an election-mail logo, high-speed scanning capability and a barcode tied to each voter, and to send voter details to a Postal Service portal for review before ballots shipped.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that applying it this year would be arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, because election officials have no reasonable time to implement it before the vote. Trump called it another bad decision and said the justices "are not the people I interviewed".
global.geopolitical: Read abroad as a test of whether American courts still constrain the executive over the conduct of an election. The answer, from a bench where three of the president's own appointees sat in the majority, was yes.
global.socioeconomic: Tens of millions of Americans vote by mail. States keep their existing envelope designs and processing for November, avoiding a rushed reprint and the spike in rejected ballots administrators had warned would follow it.

global.headline: Congo's Ebola epidemic passes 7,000 cases but appears to have peaked
summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo reported 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths as of 14 September — its largest Ebola outbreak on record and the largest ever of the Bundibugyo strain. Officials said transmission appears to have peaked in mid-August. Ituri province accounts for 5,659 cases and 2,583 deaths across 28 of its 36 health zones, with new cases still reported in North Kivu and Haut-Uélé.

The outbreak passed 1,000 cases within 40 days of the response being activated; the 2018 epidemic took about 235 days to reach that mark. There is no licensed vaccine or treatment for Bundibugyo, and health workers began receiving Ervebo — licensed against a different Ebola species — from 27 August.
global.geopolitical: A peak is not an end, and Ebola outbreaks are lost in the tail. The worst-hit provinces are also the least governed, which is why the response took months to reach the scale the case curve had already demanded.
global.socioeconomic: The gap exposed here is product, not logistics: the world has a licensed vaccine for one Ebola species and none for the others. Trial data gathered in this outbreak will decide whether that changes before the next one.

singapore.headline: Ransomware hits the payroll system used by mosques and madrasahs
summary: The SmartHRMS human-resource system used by mosques and madrasahs under the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (Muis) was hit by ransomware, with threat-actor activity first detected on 30 and 31 August. The system is believed to have held the names, contact details, salaries and bank account numbers of staff at dozens of institutions.

Accounting staff were locked out and processed salaries by hand while business-continuity arrangements were put in place, and affected employees are being given guidance. Muis declined to say how many mosques and madrasahs were involved, precisely what data was compromised, whether a ransom was paid or whether any data has been recovered, citing ongoing investigations. The system is supplied by Singapore software vendor Avelogic.
singapore.geopolitical: Limited, but the target matters. Religious bodies sit outside the critical information infrastructure regime that protects banks and utilities, and an attack on Muslim community institutions invites a communal reading whatever the attackers intended.
singapore.socioeconomic: One vendor served dozens of institutions, so a single breach exposed all of them at once. Small charities and religious bodies buy shared software precisely because they cannot run their own — that is the concentration risk.

singapore.headline: Parliament is not a firm's risk committee, Foo says on Air India
summary: Minister of State for Trade and Industry Foo Cexiang told Parliament its role is to hold the government accountable, not to serve as "the risk committee for individual companies". He rejected Workers' Party MP Kenneth Tiong's framing of Parliament as the reserves' risk function with Singapore Airlines' board as the investment team, calling it a major leap of logic.

Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said Air India's losses do not automatically become SIA's liabilities and that its latest request for fresh equity does not oblige SIA to provide it. SIA holds 25.1 per cent of Air India, which lost about S$3 billion (US$2.33 billion) in the year to March 2026 and is seeking roughly S$1.9 billion (US$1.5 billion) from shareholders.
singapore.geopolitical: SIA's largest foreign bet sits inside India's aviation market, and Delhi's consolidation of Air India is partly underwritten from Singapore. How the stake is handled will be read in India as a signal about Singaporean staying power.
singapore.socioeconomic: The live question went unanswered. If SIA declines to fund its 25.1 per cent share its stake dilutes; if it funds, Temasek's ultimate exposure to a loss-making carrier grows. Neither outcome is Parliament's to decide.

singapore.headline: Haze eases to one unhealthy region as clinics report more asthma flare-ups
summary: Air quality improved through Tuesday and overnight. The 24-hour PSI in the east, west, north and south fell back into the moderate band, leaving only the central region above 101 by early Wednesday — a day after all five regions crossed into the unhealthy range for the first time since 2019 and the central reading reached 154.

Doctors reported roughly 20 per cent more patients with asthma flare-ups, nose allergies and throat irritation, and organisations moved activities indoors and distributed masks. Experts attributed the central region's persistently worse readings partly to dense urbanisation and stronger urban heat. The smoke continues to blow in from fires in Kalimantan and southern Sumatra.
singapore.geopolitical: Indonesia's fires are burning into an El Niño the WMO expects to last into February, and the smoke now covers four countries. No enforcement action under the ASEAN transboundary haze agreement has followed this season.
singapore.socioeconomic: A fifth more respiratory cases is the visible cost; outdoor work is the hidden one. Singapore's heat-stress measures become mandatory in December, but no equivalent trigger halts work on air quality alone.

singapore.headline: First seized properties from the S$3b laundering case go under the hammer
summary: The first real estate forfeited in the S$3 billion money-laundering case reaches auction this week: seven properties at Knight Frank on 17 September, then nine at Edmund Tie and ten at SRI on 23 September. Guide prices run from S$2.238 million for a Martin Modern unit to S$25.3 million for a South Beach Residences penthouse of more than 6,700 sq ft, with a Grade A office at Suntec Tower One listed at S$11.5 million.
Deloitte is managing the disposal of more than 80 properties and Hotlotz is running 15 auctions of over 1,000 luxury items through to mid-2027. Proceeds go to the Consolidated Fund.
singapore.geopolitical: The disposal is the visible end of a case that began as a question about who was allowed to bank here. Foreign counterparts will read the amount actually recovered as the measure of whether the enforcement was real.
singapore.socioeconomic: Twenty-six prime units arriving at once is small against total supply but concentrated in a thin segment, and the guide prices look set to clear the stock rather than to test the top of the market.

singapore.headline: Retailers slash drink prices before the Return Right deposit mark becomes compulsory
summary: Supermarkets and convenience chains are discounting beer, tea and other canned and bottled drinks that do not carry the Return Right deposit mark — some at half price — to clear stock before 1 October. From that date it becomes an offence to supply any regulated beverage without the deposit mark and barcode.

Regulated beverages are pre-packaged drinks in plastic or metal containers holding 150ml to 3 litres. The deadline ends the six-month transition that began when the Beverage Container Return Scheme and its 10-cent deposit took effect on 1 April. Unmarked stock cannot lawfully be sold after the cut-off, whether or not the seller collects the deposit.
singapore.geopolitical: Slight, beyond the regional plastics debate: Singapore is the first in South-east Asia to run a national container deposit, and neighbours weighing their own schemes are watching the return rates rather than the drafting.
singapore.socioeconomic: The discounting is the transition working as intended — the cost of unsold stock falls on retailers, not on the scheme. Shoppers get a fortnight of cheap drinks and then a 10-cent deposit on every can.

word.definition: Military equipment, weapons and supplies, as distinct from personnel.
word.etymology: From French matériel, "equipment", from Latin materia, "matter, stuff".
word.example: The budget office priced six months of war in materiel: US$21.7 billion of munitions and five years to refill the interceptor magazines.
